steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our NLP paper on DepWiGNN, a depth-wise graph neural network for multi-hop spatial reasoning in text. It should explain why textual spatial reasoning matters and is hard, why earlier memory-based models and standard GNNs fall short, how our method works at a high level, and end with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Spatial reasoning in text: why it matters, why it is hard, newer benchmarks
- Prior approach: TPR-based recurrent memory network and its limits
- GNNs for multi-hop reasoning: over-smoothing and breadth aggregation
- Our method: DepWiGNN (depth-wise propagation with TPR node memory)
- Experimental findings
- Contributions (three)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Spatial reasoning in text: why it matters, why it is hard, newer benchmarks
  - crucial in many areas: medical domain, navigation, robotics (cite each)
  - challenging for PLMs (cite) and LLMs like ChatGPT (cite)
  - early datasets e.g. bAbI (cite): over-simple, don't reflect real textual spatial reasoning
  - recent benchmarks (cite): more complex, more reasoning steps, more varied spatial relation expressions
  - Figure 1 example: 4 reasoning steps, diverse relation descriptions/categories
- Prior approach: TPR-based recurrent memory network
  - prior work (cite) proposes recurrent memory network based on Tensor Product Representation (TPR) (cite)
  - mimics step-by-step reasoning; iteratively updates/removes episodes from memory
  - TPR: encodes symbolic knowledge from natural language into distributed vector space for deductive reasoning
  - but outperformed by modern PLMs (cite)
  - these works overlook gap between natural language and symbolic relations
- GNNs for multi-hop reasoning
  - widely used for multi-hop reasoning (cite)
  - one graph conv layer (node -> immediate neighbors) = one reasoning step; stack layers for multi-hop
  - more layers can hurt performance (cite): over-smoothing, adjacent nodes become more similar each layer
  - paradox: need many layers for multi-hop dependencies, but stacking them fails because of over-smoothing
  - chain-finding problems (e.g. multi-hop spatial reasoning) only need a specific depth path, not full breadth aggregation over all neighbors (Figure 1)
  - existing methods (cite) rely on iterated breadth aggregation -> superfluous/irrelevant info distracts model
- Our method: DepWiGNN
  - Depth-Wise Graph Neural Network; operates over depth instead of breadth dimension
  - novel node memory storing only depth path info between nodes, via TPR
  - init: fill atomic info (spatial relation) between each pair of directly connected nodes
  - then: relation between indirectly connected nodes by depth-wise retrieving + aggregating atomic relations along the path
  - store collected long-dependency info in source node memory; retrieve freely given target node
  - unlike typical GNNs (cite): no stacking needed -> immune to over-smoothing
  - prioritizes key path info instead of aimless breadth aggregation over all neighbors
- Experimental findings
  - two challenging multi-hop spatial reasoning datasets
  - beats existing spatial reasoning methods; also enhances PLMs' spatial reasoning
  - vs three GNNs: better at long dependencies by noticeable margin, short dependency collection not harmed
- Contributions (three)
  - DepWiGNN: propagation over depth, long dependency without stacking, avoids over-smoothing
  - node memory scheme with TPR: update/retrieval by simple arithmetic, not neural layers
  - strong results on two datasets; comparisons with three GNNs; code at https://github.com/Syon-Li/DepWiGNN

steps.text:

It has been shown to be a hard problem both for modern pre-trained language models (PLMs) and for large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT. Early datasets for textual spatial reasoning, like bAbI, are too simple, so they cannot really show the real textual spatial reasoning scenario. Recently researchers have proposed several new benchmarks that are more complex: they need more reasoning steps, the spatial relations are expressed in more varied ways, and so on. In the example in Figure 1, 4 steps of reasoning are needed to answer the question, and the spatial relation descriptions and categories are diverse.

For multi-hop spatial reasoning, one prior work proposes a recurrent memory network that is based on Tensor Product Representation (TPR). The model imitates step-by-step reasoning by updating and removing episodes from memory iteratively. TPR encodes the symbolic knowledge hidden in natural language into a distributed vector space so that it can be used for deductive reasoning. Using TPR memory is effective, but this model is still beaten by modern PLMs. These works also usually overlook the gap between natural language and symbolic relations.

- GNNs for multi-hop reasoning
  - widely used (cite); one graph conv layer = one reasoning step; stack layers for multi-hop
  - more layers hurt (cite): over-smoothing, adjacent nodes become more similar
  - paradox: need many layers but stacking fails
  - chain-finding problems only need a specific depth path, not full breadth aggregation (Figure 1)
  - existing methods (cite) rely on breadth aggregation -> irrelevant info distracts model
- Our method: DepWiGNN
  - operates over depth instead of breadth; TPR node memory storing depth path info
  - init with atomic spatial relations between directly connected nodes; depth-wise retrieve + aggregate along path; store in source node memory
  - unlike typical GNNs (cite): no stacking, immune to over-smoothing; prioritizes key path info
- Experimental findings: two datasets, beats spatial reasoning methods, helps PLMs; better than three GNNs on long dependencies

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Spatial reasoning in text is important in a lot of areas, for example the medical domain, navigation and robotics. It has been shown to be a hard problem both for modern pre-trained language models (PLMs) and for large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT. Early datasets for textual spatial reasoning, like bAbI, are too simple, so they cannot really show the real textual spatial reasoning scenario. Recently researchers have proposed several new benchmarks that are more complex: they need more reasoning steps, the spatial relations are expressed in more varied ways, and so on. In the example in Figure 1, 4 steps of reasoning are needed to answer the question, and the spatial relation descriptions and categories are diverse.

For multi-hop spatial reasoning, one prior work proposes a recurrent memory network that is based on Tensor Product Representation (TPR). The model imitates step-by-step reasoning by updating and removing episodes from memory iteratively. TPR encodes the symbolic knowledge hidden in natural language into a distributed vector space so that it can be used for deductive reasoning. Using TPR memory is effective, but this model is still beaten by modern PLMs. These works also usually overlook the gap between natural language and symbolic relations.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been used a lot in multi-hop reasoning. Usually these methods treat one graph convolutional layer, where node information is propagated to the node's immediate neighbors, as one step of reasoning, and they get multi-hop reasoning by stacking several layers. But having more graph convolutional layers in deep neural structures can hurt model performance. This is called the over-smoothing problem, and it happens because every layer of graph convolutions makes adjacent nodes more similar to each other. So there is a paradox for multi-hop reasoning: you need multiple layers to capture multi-hop dependencies, but if you use them they can fail to capture these dependencies because of over-smoothing. Also, many chain-finding problems like multi-hop spatial reasoning only need the information of a specific depth path to answer a question, and they do not need full breadth aggregation over all neighbors (Figure 1). Existing methods for this kind of problem still usually do propagation by iterating breadth aggregation, which brings in extra and irrelevant information that can distract the model from the key information.

Because of these problems, we propose a new graph-based method called Depth-Wise Graph Neural Network (DepWiGNN). It works over the depth dimension of the graph instead of the breadth dimension to solve the multi-hop spatial reasoning problem. It uses a new node memory implementation that only stores the depth path information between nodes, using the TPR technique. First it initializes the node memory by filling in the atomic information (the spatial relation) between each pair of directly connected nodes. Then it gets the relation between two indirectly connected nodes by retrieving and aggregating, depth-wise, all the atomic spatial relations stored in the memory of each node on the path. The long-dependency information that is collected is then stored in the memory of the source node of the path and can be retrieved freely when the target node is given. Typical existing GNNs need to be stacked to get long relationships between two distant nodes, but DepWiGNN does not, so it is immune to the over-smoothing problem. And instead of doing breadth aggregation on all immediate neighbors without aim, it selectively prioritizes the key path information.

We run experiments on two challenging multi-hop spatial reasoning datasets, and DepWiGNN outperforms existing spatial reasoning methods and also improves the spatial reasoning capability of PLMs. We also compare with three GNNs, and DepWiGNN is better than classical graph convolutional layers at capturing long dependencies by a noticeable margin, and it does not hurt the performance of collecting short dependencies.

Our contributions are these three:

- We propose a new graph-based method, DepWiGNN, that does propagation over the depth dimension of a graph, so it can capture long dependency without stacking layers and it avoids over-smoothing.

- We implement a new node memory scheme that uses the TPR mechanism, so memory updating and retrieval can be done with simple arithmetic operations instead of neural layers.

- DepWiGNN does very well on multi-hop spatial reasoning tasks and beats existing methods on two challenging datasets. Comparisons with three other GNNs also show it is better at capturing long dependencies in the graph. Our code will be released via https://github.com/Syon-Li/DepWiGNN.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Spatial reasoning in text is crucial in many areas, e.g., medical domain [1,2], navigations [3,4,5] and robotics [6,7]. It has been shown to be a challenging problem for both modern pre-trained language models (PLMs) [8,9] and large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT [10]. However, early textual spatial reasoning datasets, e.g., bAbI [11], suffer from over-simplicity and are therefore not qualified for revealing the real textual spatial reasoning scenario. Recently, researchers propose several new benchmarks [12,13,8] with increased complexity, which involve more required reasoning steps, more variety in spatial relation expression, and more. As shown in Figure 1, 4 steps of reasoning are needed to answer the question, and the spatial relation descriptions and categories are diverse.

To tackle multi-hop spatial reasoning, [12] propose a recurrent memory network based on Tensor Product Representation (TPR) [14], which mimics step-by-step reasoning by iteratively updating and removing episodes from memory. Specifically, TPR encodes symbolic knowledge hidden in natural language into a distributed vector space to be used for deductive reasoning. Despite the effectiveness of TPR memory, the performance of this model is overwhelmed by modern PLMs [13]. Moreover, these works typically overlook the gap between natural language and symbolic relations.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been considerably used in multi-hop reasoning [15,16,17]. These methods often treat a single graph convolutional layer of node information propagation (node to its immediate neighbors) as one step of reasoning and extend it to multi-hop reasoning by stacking multiple layers. However, increasing the number of graph convolutional layers in deep neural structures can harm model performance [18]. This phenomenon, known as the over-smoothing problem, occurs because each layer of graph convolutions makes adjacent nodes more similar to each other. This creates a paradox for multi-hop reasoning: although multiple layers are needed to capture multi-hop dependencies, implementing them can fail to capture these dependencies because of over-smoothing. Furthermore, many chain-finding problems, e.g., multi-hop spatial reasoning, only require specific depth path information to solve a single question and do not need full breadth aggregation over all neighbors (Figure 1). Nevertheless, existing methods [19,15,16,20] for this kind of problem usually rely on propagation by iterations of breadth aggregation, which brings superfluous and irrelevant information that may distract the model from the key information.

In light of these challenges, we propose a novel graph-based method, named Depth-Wise Graph Neural Network (DepWiGNN), which operates over the depth instead of the breadth dimension of the graph to tackle the multi-hop spatial reasoning problem. It introduces a novel node memory implementation that only stores depth path information between nodes by applying the TPR technique. Specifically, it first initializes the node memory by filling in the atomic information (spatial relation) between each pair of directly connected nodes, and then collects the relation between two indirectly connected nodes by depth-wise retrieving and aggregating all atomic spatial relations stored in the memory of each node in the path. The collected long-dependency information is then stored in the source node memory of the path and can be retrieved freely if the target node is given. Unlike typical existing GNNs [21,22,23,24], DepWiGNN does not need to be stacked to obtain long relationships between two distant nodes and is therefore immune to the over-smoothing problem. Moreover, rather than aimlessly performing breadth aggregation on all immediate neighbors, it selectively prioritizes the key path information.

Experiments on two challenging multi-hop spatial reasoning datasets show that DepWiGNN not only outperforms existing spatial reasoning methods but also enhances the spatial reasoning capability of PLMs. Comparisons with three GNNs show that DepWiGNN surpasses classical graph convolutional layers in capturing long dependencies by a noticeable margin, without harming the performance of short dependency collection.

Overall, our contributions are threefold:

- We propose a novel graph-based method, DepWiGNN, which performs propagation over the depth dimension of a graph, capturing long dependency without stacking layers and avoiding the issue of over-smoothing.

- We implement a novel node memory scheme that takes advantage of the TPR mechanism, allowing memory updating and retrieval through simple arithmetic operations instead of neural layers.

- DepWiGNN excels in multi-hop spatial reasoning tasks, surpassing existing methods on two challenging datasets. In addition, comparisons with three other GNNs highlight its superior ability to capture long dependencies within the graph. Our code will be released via https://github.com/Syon-Li/DepWiGNN.

References:

Understanding spatial language in radiology: Representation framework, annotation, and spatial relation extraction from chest x-ray reports using deep learning . J. Biomed. Informatics , 108:103473.
